title: Faster patching is also a risk: Microsoft president warns the perfect storm will come again

content_html:
The global internet has suffered a string of outages recently: Microsoft Exchange, Outlook, and Teams experienced widespread failures, while Apple's App Store, multiple banks, airlines, and PlayStation Network also went down one after another. On November 24, reports said that Microsoft President Brad Smith had warned in a November 22 post that the risk of global technical failures will remain high in the coming months. Officials have ruled out the possibility of a coordinated cyberattack, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said there is no evidence that the incidents are related to one another.

AI Is Making Patches Outpace Testing

Smith believes AI is changing the pace of cybersecurity and system operations: security teams can use it to find code vulnerabilities more easily, while malicious attackers also use it to find entry points. As a result, companies are forced to deploy patches at "unprecedented speed," leaving much less time for testing and validation. He singled out aging infrastructure as the most vulnerable: when updates are rushed and testing is insufficient, patches meant to improve security can instead trigger new failures. Microsoft's recent global outage was attributed to a "perfect storm" created by a software update four months earlier, newer updates, and changes in network traffic.

During Upgrades, Outages Won't Stop

More troubling, Smith noted that "the entire global information infrastructure is in fact undergoing upgrades and renovations," and the related risks cannot be resolved in a few weeks; more technical failures are likely in the months ahead. In other words, for some time to come, the cycle of "find a vulnerability—rush out a patch—the patch creates a new problem" may play out again and again. Compared with patching speed, system resilience has become the scarcer resource.
